title: Brute Force Strategy
description: How **brute force** solves problems by checking every possibility -- correct by construction, but expensive at scale.

sections.title: Introduction to Exhaustive Enumeration
sections.content:
The most direct way to solve a problem: check every possible candidate. That's the **Brute Force** strategy.

No heuristics, no caching, no math shortcuts -- just sequential checking of every candidate until the answer is found or the search space runs out.

Brute force matters because it's usually your **first correct solution**. Dynamic programming, divide-and-conquer, and greedy algorithms are often just optimized versions of an initial brute-force idea -- understanding the exhaustive version is how you spot where to optimize.

sections.title: The Engineering Value of Brute Force
sections.content:
A brute-force implementation gives you a **trusted baseline** -- correct output on small inputs that you can check faster algorithms against.

It also makes the whole search space visible: checking every combination lets you spot redundant work and memory issues directly. And on small, bounded inputs (a 4-element config array, a tiny state machine), brute force is genuinely the right tool -- no risk, no overhead.
bullets: A **correct baseline** for testing faster algorithms.
Covers the **full search space** -- no missed edge cases.

sections.title: The Core Mechanics of Systematic Testing
sections.content:
The core idea: **deterministic, systematic iteration**. No jumping around based on sorted order or probability -- just sequential checking.

For arrays, that means index 0 to n-1 in order. For combinatorial problems (like finding a pair that sums to a target), it means nested loops generating every combination.

Because every candidate gets checked, brute force **mathematically guarantees** a correct answer on any finite search space -- there's no risk of an optimization heuristic skipping the right one.

sections.title: Brute Force in Searching
sections.content:
The classic example: **Linear Scan**. Looking for a value in an unsorted list means starting at index 0 and checking each one in turn -- the only option, since there's no sorted structure to exploit.

That's what makes it brute force: worst case, it checks 100% of the data. It stops early on a match (an easy optimization), or runs to the end and returns "not found."

sections.title: Implementation Examples
sections.content:
Brute force leans on basic loops, tracking variables, and comparisons.

**Extrema Tracking:** start a tracker at the first element, then compare each remaining element against it, updating when you find something bigger (or smaller). O(n).

**Combinatorial Pairing:** an outer loop plus a nested inner loop checks every pair for a target sum. Since the inner loop runs fully for each outer step, that's O(n²).

**Conditional Aggregation & Early Exit:** counting evens with a modulo check is a full O(n) pass; finding the *first* negative number can return the instant it's found, which helps average case while the worst case stays O(n).

sections.title: Understanding Exhaustive Search
sections.content:
Brute force is also called **exhaustive search** -- nothing is skipped, everything is checked methodically.

The cost depends on what's being enumerated: a linear scan is O(n), checking every sub-array pushes to O(n²), and checking every subset of a set is O(2^n). At n=20, that's ~1,000,000 branches; at n=40, over 1,000,000,000,000 -- a hard wall for exponential brute force.

Correctness is guaranteed. Scalability is not.

chart.description: Brute force often starts linear, but combinations and nested checks push it toward quadratic or exponential.

sections.title: Backtracking: Smart Brute Force
sections.content:
Generating every full candidate up front (like all N-Queens boards) can blow up memory fast. **Backtracking** fixes this: build a candidate incrementally, and the moment a partial choice fails, abandon that branch immediately instead of finishing it.

That "choose, explore, prune, unchoose" loop skips huge chunks of the search space before ever computing them -- exhaustive correctness, without the memory blowup.

sections.title: Time and Space Complexity
sections.content:
One loop over n items → O(n) time. A loop nested inside another → O(n²). Generating all subsets → O(2^n).

Simple aggregations (extrema, counting) use a fixed number of trackers regardless of input size -- **O(1) space**.

More complex searches cost more: storing all candidates is O(n) space, tracking visited states can be O(n) or O(n²), and recursive combination generation needs O(depth) stack space -- watch for stack overflow if unbounded.

sections.title: Brute Force vs Optimized Algorithms
sections.content:
The difference: brute force ignores data structure and just checks everything; optimized algorithms exploit structure to skip work.

Unsorted array search: brute force O(n). Sort it first, then Binary Search cuts the search space in half each step -- O(log n). At 1 million items: ~1,000,000 checks vs. ~20 -- **50,000x faster**.

Same story for pair-matching: brute force is O(n²) from nested loops, but a Hash Map turns the inner loop into an O(1) lookup, dropping the whole thing to O(n).

Use brute force when **n is small**, **correctness matters most**, or you need a **baseline**. Use optimized algorithms when **n is large** or **performance matters**.

subsections.title: Advantages
bullets: Great for **debugging and testing** faster solutions.

subsections.title: Limitations
bullets: Often **impractical** for large or real-time systems.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Brute force shows up when input is small, correctness matters most, or optimizing just isn't worth the effort.

**Password testing:** security tools try every combination in a character set -- slow, but guaranteed to find it if it's in range.

**Small game AI:** Tic-Tac-Toe's state space is small enough that an AI can check every move and play perfectly.

**Configuration testing:** with only a few settings, testing every combination to find a bug or best config is entirely feasible.

**Competitive programming:** many beginner problems are sized specifically so a brute-force solution passes within the time limit.

subsections.title: Misconception: Brute force is always bad
subsections.content: For under ~100 elements, a fancy balanced tree or hash map often costs more overhead than it saves. Brute force can genuinely be the *faster* choice at small scale -- the problem only shows up as the search space grows.

subsections.title: Misconception: Brute force is always O(n)
subsections.content: Brute force describes a *method* (check everything), not a fixed complexity. Depending on what's enumerated, it can land at O(n²), O(n³), or even O(n!).

subsections.title: Misconception: Brute force means random guessing
subsections.content: It's the opposite -- **strictly deterministic and systematic**, methodically covering every candidate with no repeats and no skips. Random guessing can miss things; brute force can't.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Brute force solves problems by **systematically checking every candidate**.
Cost depends on **how many candidates get tested**.
Large search spaces can make it **impractical** -- watch for quadratic or exponential blowup.
